opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the physical world isn't only something you see.

When we started the Cosmos effort, vision was the natural entry point. Video is abundant, it carries a huge amount of information about how objects move and interact, and a model that can predict plausible future frames has learned something real about physics. But if you want a world model to be useful for physical AI, for robots, autonomous vehicles, or any agent that acts in the world, vision alone leaves gaps.

Think about how a robot picks up a cup. Vision tells you where the cup is and roughly what shape it has. It doesn't tell you how heavy it is, whether it's slipping, or how much force the gripper is applying. That comes from touch, force-torque sensing, and proprioception, the robot's sense of its own joints. A self-driving car combines cameras with lidar, radar, and its own motion signals. Humans are the same: we hear a glass crack before we see it break, and we feel resistance before we notice anything visually. If a world model only understands pixels, it can only reason about part of what's happening.

There's also the question of conditioning and control. A world model isn't just a video generator; it's a simulator you can query. You want to say "what happens if the robot takes this action?" or "what if the road is wet?" That means the model has to accept actions, trajectories, language instructions, maybe structured signals like depth or segmentation, and connect them to its predictions. The more of these modalities it understands, the more precisely developers can steer it and the more useful it is for generating training data or evaluating policies.

Finally, there's a generalization argument. Different modalities constrain each other. If the model has to keep vision, sound, and physical interaction consistent with one another, it's pushed toward an internal representation that reflects the underlying physics rather than surface statistics of one data type. We think that's a path toward models that hold up better in situations they haven't seen.

So moving beyond vision isn't about adding features for their own sake. It's about getting closer to how the world actually is, and to the kinds of information an embodied agent actually needs to act well in it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simple reason is that the physical world is not just something you see. A robot or an autonomous vehicle operating in the world experiences it through many channels at once. There's vision, yes, but there's also sound, there's touch, there's force and torque feedback from the joints, there's proprioception, the sense of where your own body is in space. If you build a world model that only understands pixels, you are giving the machine one sense and asking it to reason about a world that humans navigate with five or six.

Think about a humanoid picking up a cup. The camera tells you the cup is there. But whether the cup is full or empty, whether it is slipping, whether you are squeezing too hard, that information mostly comes through the hand, through contact. Vision alone is often ambiguous about exactly the things that matter most for manipulation. So if the world model cannot take those signals as input, it cannot predict what happens next with the fidelity the robot actually needs.

The second reason is about grounding and control. We want people to be able to condition the model on language, on actions, on the state of the robot, on previous trajectories. A world model is really a simulator, and a simulator is only useful if you can tell it what situation to simulate. Language is how a human expresses intent. Actions are how the policy expresses what it wants to try. Sensor state is how the model knows where it is starting from. All of those have to come in together, in the same model, so that the prediction is consistent across modalities. If vision says one thing and the force sensor says another, the model should learn that relationship instead of being blind to it.

And honestly there is a practical dimension too. Our partners building robots have very different sensor suites. Some have depth, some have LiDAR, some have tactile skins, some are mostly cameras. We did not want to build a model that only works for one hardware configuration. So we designed Cosmos 3 to be flexible about what it ingests, so it can be useful across that whole range and improve as more kinds of data become available.

So for me it is not really a feature. It is what it means to model the physical world rather than to model video. Video is a window onto the world. The world itself is much richer than the window.

astra-6.text:
Because vision only captures part of what’s happening in the world. You can see an object move, but that alone may not tell you what caused it to move, what action was taken, or what forces were involved. If we want a world model to help an embodied system understand and interact with its environment, it needs to connect what it sees with actions and other signals.

Think about a robot picking up a cup. The camera gives it information about the cup’s position, but touch can tell it whether the grip is secure. Language can tell it what the person wants done with the cup. Accepting inputs beyond vision lets the model bring those pieces together, so it can predict what happens next in a way that’s useful for taking action.

sol-6.1.text: Vision gives you a lot of information, but it doesn’t tell you everything about the state of the world. If you want a world model to help a robot predict what happens next, it also needs to understand the robot’s actions and other available signals. The same visual scene can evolve very differently depending on what action you take. Accepting inputs beyond vision lets the model condition its predictions on that additional context, which makes it more useful for physical AI.
